title: Personalized Large Language Models Can Increase the Belief Accuracy of Social Networks
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in shaping public
understanding on contested issues. This has led to substantial discussion about
the potential of LLMs to reinforce or correct misperceptions. While existing
literature documents the impact of LLMs on individuals' beliefs, limited work
explores how LLMs affect social networks. We address this gap with a
pre-registered experiment (N = 1265) around the 2024 US presidential election,
where we empirically explore the impact of personalized LLMs on belief accuracy
in the context of social networks. The LLMs are constructed to be personalized,
offering messages tailored to individuals' profiles, and to have guardrails for
accurate information retrieval. We find that the presence of a personalized LLM
leads individuals to update their beliefs towards the truth. More importantly,
individuals with a personalized LLM in their social network not only choose to
follow it, indicating they would like to obtain information from it in
subsequent interactions, but also construct subsequent social networks to
include other individuals with beliefs similar to the LLM -- in this case, more
accurate beliefs. Therefore, our results show that LLMs have the capacity to
influence individual beliefs and the social networks in which people exist, and
highlight the potential of LLMs to act as corrective agents in online
environments. Our findings can inform future strategies for responsible
AI-mediated communication.

bib.abstract: This study examines whether personality traits predict an individual's perceived accuracy and sharing intention of political misinformation and if cognitive ability further moderates this relationship. An analysis of survey data from the US revealed that individuals with high agreeableness and low extraversion were more likely to discern pro-conservative misinformation correctly. Individuals with high agreeableness and conscientiousness were also less likely to share partisan misinformation. Further, individuals with high cognitive ability were more likely to discern correctly and less likely to share misinformation across the partisan spectrum. Moderation analyses suggest that low cognitive individuals with higher neuroticism and openness are more prone to sharing partisan misinformation. However, high levels of agreeableness can safeguard low cognitive individuals from sharing. We discuss the implications of this work for theorizing misinformation engagement and its effects.

bib.abstractnote: Background: The development of COVID-19 vaccines has been crucial in fighting the pandemic. However, misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccines is spread on social media platforms at a rate that has made the World Health Organization coin the phrase infodemic. False claims about adverse vaccine side effects, such as vaccines being the cause of autism, were already considered a threat to global health before the outbreak of COVID-19. Objective: We aimed to synthesize the existing research on misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines spread on social media platforms and its effects. The secondary aim was to gain insight and gather knowledge about whether misinformation about autism and COVID-19 vaccines is being spread on social media platforms. Methods: We performed a literature search on September 9, 2021, and searched PubMed, PsycINFO, ERIC, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, and the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register. We included publications in peer-reviewed journals that fulfilled the following criteria: original empirical studies, studies that assessed social media and misinformation, and studies about COVID-19 vaccines. Thematic analysis was used to identify the patterns (themes) of misinformation. Narrative qualitative synthesis was undertaken with the guidance of the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) 2020 Statement and the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis reporting guideline. The risk of bias was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal tool. Ratings of the certainty of evidence were based on recommendations from the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation Working Group. Results: The search yielded 757 records, with 45 articles selected for this review. We identified 3 main themes of misinformation: medical misinformation, vaccine development, and conspiracies. Twitter was the most studied social media platform, followed by Facebook, YouTube, and Instagram. A vast majority of studies were from industrialized Western countries. We identified 19 studies in which the effect of social media misinformation on vaccine hesitancy was measured or discussed. These studies implied that the misinformation spread on social media had a negative effect on vaccine hesitancy and uptake. Only 1 study contained misinformation about autism as a side effect of COVID-19 vaccines. Conclusions: To prevent these misconceptions from taking hold, health authorities should openly address and discuss these false claims with both cultural and religious awareness in mind. Our review showed that there is a need to examine the effect of social media misinformation on vaccine hesitancy with a more robust experimental design. Furthermore, this review also demonstrated that more studies are needed from the Global South and on social media platforms other than the major platforms such as Twitter and Facebook. bib.abstractnote: Despite its importance to society and many decades of research, key questions about the social and psychological processes of political persuasion remain unanswered, often due to data limitations. We propose that AI tools, specifically generative large language models (LLMs), can be used to address these limitations, offering important advantages in the study of political persuasion. In two preregistered online survey experiments, we demonstrate the potential of generative AI as a tool to study persuasion and provide important insights about the psychological and communicative processes that lead to increased persuasion. Specifically, we test the effects of four AI-generated counterattitudinal persuasive strategies, designed to test the effectiveness of messages that include customization (writing messages based on a receiver’s personal traits and beliefs), and elaboration (increased psychological engagement with the argument through interaction). We find that all four types of persuasive AI produce significant attitude change relative to the control and shift vote support for candidates espousing views consistent with the treatments. However, we do not find evidence that message customization via microtargeting or cognitive elaboration through interaction with the AI have much more persuasive effect than a single generic message. These findings have implications for different theories of persuasion, which we discuss. Finally, we find that although persuasive messages are able to moderate some people’s attitudes, they have inconsistent and weaker effects on the democratic reciprocity people grant to their political opponents. This suggests that attitude moderation (ideological depolarization) does not necessarily lead to increased democratic tolerance or decreased affective polarization.
bib.title: Testing theories of political persuasion using AI

bib.abstractnote:
Issues of attitudes and attitude change are the foundation of many social processes. Psychologists have long sought to understand people’s opinions and evaluations and many studies have sought to understand how, why, and when those attitudes change in the face of persuasive communication. Early persuasion research identified many variables that influence the effectiveness of persuasive messages. These variables include characteristics of the communicator, the recipient, and the message itself. Over the years, however, the evidence for these influences became rather mixed, prompting a new generation of persuasion psychologists to ask whether there was a sensible pattern underlying it.

This question ushered in several new approaches to thinking about persuasion. These “dual process” models proposed key moderators, identifying the conditions under which certain variables would and would not produce attitude change. A particularly influential model has been the
Elaboration Likelihood Model
(ELM), which proposed that the audience’s motivation and ability to think deeply about a persuasive message determines how much a given characteristic of that message will change the audience’s attitude. Other models, such as the
Heuristic-Systematic Model
(HSM), have contributed additional insights about the “when” and “why” of attitude change. In sum, these nuanced accounts of attitude change have been demonstrated time and again across cultures and topics of persuasion.
bib.title: Dual process models of persuasion

\begin{abstract} \bfseries \boldmath

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in shaping public understanding on contested issues. This has led to substantial discussion about the potential of LLMs to reinforce or correct misperceptions. While existing literature documents the impact of LLMs on individuals’ beliefs, limited work explores how LLMs affect social networks. We address this gap with a pre-registered experiment (N = 1265) around the 2024 U.S. presidential election, where we empirically explore the impact of personalized LLMs on belief accuracy in the context of social networks. The LLMs are constructed to be personalized, offering messages tailored to individuals’ profiles, and to have guardrails for accurate information retrieval. We find that the presence of a personalized LLM leads individuals to update their beliefs towards the truth. More importantly, individuals with a personalized LLM in their social network not only choose to follow it (as a way of indicating they would like to obtain information from it in subsequent interactions), but also construct subsequent social networks to include other individuals with beliefs similar to the LLM – in this case, more accurate beliefs. Therefore, our results show that LLMs have the capacity to influence individual beliefs and the social networks in which people exist, and highlight the potential of LLMs to act as corrective agents in online environments. Our findings can inform future strategies for responsible AI-mediated communication.

The LLMs are constructed to be personalized, offering messages tailored to individuals’ profiles, and to have guardrails for accurate information retrieval. First, we find that the presence of a personalized LLM leads individuals to update their beliefs towards the truth. Second, individuals with a personalized LLM in their social network not only choose to follow it, but also construct subsequent social networks to include other individuals with beliefs similar to the LLM – in this case, more accurate beliefs. Therefore, our results show that LLMs have the capacity to influence not only beliefs but also the social networks in which people exist, and highlight the potential of LLMs to act as corrective agents in online environments. %Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly involved in shaping public understanding on contested issues, raising questions about their potential to reinforce or correct misperceptions. We explore the impact of personalized LLMs (i.e., one that offers messages tailored to individuals’ profiles) on belief accuracy in the context of social networks. We find that the presence of a personalized LLM with guardrails (i.e., constructed to offer accurate information) increases the accuracy of individuals’ beliefs in the network. Moreover, the likelihood that individuals construct subsequent networks that consist of others with more accurate beliefs increases within the treatment condition. We offer clear evidence for these predictions with a pre-registered experiment (N = 1265) around the 2024 U.S. presidential election. The results make clear that the personalized LLM can prompt movement toward accuracy and can lead people to construct social networks that include others with accurate beliefs. The findings highlight the potential of LLMs to act as corrective agents in online environments and inform future strategies for responsible AI-mediated communication.

\end{abstract}



\noindent

Misinformed beliefs pose major challenges across a range of domains, from public health and civic trust to the understanding of basic facts \cite{nyhan2020facts, matatov2022stop, oehmichen2019not, bovet2019influence}. These beliefs can erode confidence in voting systems \cite{lazer2018science, tucker2018social}, vaccination programs \cite{Eggertson_2010, Skafle_NordahHansen_Quintana_Wynn_Gabarron_2022}, and mainstream news organizations \cite{Ognyanova_Lazer_Robertson_Wilson_2020}. They also are often tied to misperceptions about policies and empirical reality \cite{nyhan2020facts}.

The rise of large language models (LLMs) has amplified both the risks and opportunities in this space. LLMs can generate misinformation at scale \cite{huang2024fakegpt}, sometimes producing false claims that humans find difficult to distinguish from truth \cite{chen2024can}. At the same time, LLMs are being explored for their potential to support factual accuracy through automated fact verification \cite{pan2023fact, wang2024mmidr}, disinformation detection \cite{lucasetal2023fighting}, and conversational engagement \cite{costello2024durably}.

Central to both their promise and their risk is the persuasive nature of LLMs. Empirical work has shown that LLMs can be highly persuasive on their own \cite{breum2024persuasive}, sometimes rivaling trusted human authorities such as public health agencies \cite{karinshak2023working}. LLMs can also be personalized --- that is, LLMs can structure communications to match a person’s reasoning styles \cite{costello2024durably} or psychological profiles \cite{matz2024potential}. Such personalized LLM 
messages are often more effective than general non-personalized ones \cite{matz2024potential, simchon2024persuasive}, especially if they match their audience's personality \cite{teeny2024we}, and can exert more influence than human-generated messages \cite{matz2024potential}. A crucial limitation of existing work on LLMs and belief formation is its exclusive focus on one-on-one interactions, where a user directly engages with the model in isolation \cite{costello2024durably}.
%Yet, virtually all work focuses on one-on-one interactions, where a user directly engages with the model in isolation \cite{costello2024durably}.

In reality, beliefs are rarely formed or revised in isolation. They are shaped by social context with exposure to multiple information streams \cite{PENNYCOOK2021388, Bolsen_Druckman_Cook_2014, Ahmed_Tan_2022}. Prior work has shown that social networks and peer influence play critical roles in belief formation and resistance to correction \cite{matatov2022stop, bovet2019influence, chen2021persuasion, fazio2024combating}. Despite this, little is known about how personalized LLM-generated content might function in networked environments where users are exposed to diverse and competing signals. Moreover, users actively construct their social networks, and how exposure to a personalized LLM might influence that process has gone unstudied.

Here, we study the impact of personalized LLMs in the context of a social network. The LLMs are constructed to provide accurate information, in line with work on misperception corrections \cite{porter2024factual}. Specifically, we expect that, relative to individuals in social networks without a personalized LLM, those in networks with access to a personalized LLM response will be more likely to move toward belief accuracy (hypothesis 1). This follows since the LLM will provide persuasive messaging, tailored to individual preferences. Additionally, we predict that those in social networks with an LLM are likely to include the LLM in their subsequent social network at rates greater than chance (hypothesis 2a). Prior research suggests that individuals tend to seek factual truth  \cite{pennycook2021shifting, sinclair2012social}, and LLMs, equipped with credible information, might be better able to facilitate that shift, making them desirable agents for  subsequent engagement \cite{}. Finally, this same logic (i.e., the truth-seeking nature of individuals) leads us to hypothesize that, relative to individuals in social networks without an LLM (i.e., the control), those with access to an LLM will form subsequent social networks that include significantly more members whose beliefs tend towards accuracy (hypothesis 2b). The belief updating a la hypothesis 1 combined with the desire to associate with others similar to themselves contributes to this prediction. This prediction suggests that adding an LLM to a network not only stimulates belief accuracy but it also shapes subsequent social networks such that they include more accurate beliefs overall.

Here, we evaluate our hypotheses in a dynamic, socially embedded, empirical setting (Figure~\ref{fig:ExpSchematic}). We combine three elements rarely studied together: real-time belief updated, network-mediated exposure, and personalized LLM messaging. Specifically, we were interested in whether the presence of the LLM caused participants to have more accurate beliefs, and if it impacted how participants constructed their social networks. 

In a pre-registered experiment (N = 1265) conducted from October to December 2024 (see Supplemental Materials (SM), Section \ref{part_demographics} and Tables~\ref{tab:demographics}, \ref{tab:chi2_demographics}, and \ref{tab:mwu_personality}), individuals rated on a five-point scale the extent to which they believed a randomly assigned political statement that could be objectively true or false (see SM Subsection \ref{PoliticalStatement}, and Tables~\ref{statements_part1}, \ref{statements_part2}, \ref{statements_part3}). They also provided a rationale for their belief (see SM Figure \ref{fig:stage1} for examples). Next, participants were exposed to other users' responses and had an opportunity to update their beliefs. In the control condition, participants only saw three responses from peers who had simultaneously rated the same statement. In the treatment condition, participants saw two such peer responses, and an additional personalized response from the LLM bot. Finally, in the third stage, participants were shown six overall responses. These include the responses of those they previously followed, the bot in case of treatment, and the rest randomly `recommended' by the system. Participants were instructed to follow overall three out of these six entries, and could subsequently choose to follow or unfollow others (including the bot), allowing us to observe changes in the network structure (see \textit{Materials and Methods},  and Supplemental Figures \ref{fig:stage1}, \ref{fig:stage2}, \ref{fig:stage3}). Participants were told they may or may not interact with an LLM bot in the experiment, and had provided consent to this setup. All experiments were hosted in real time with 10-28 participants, based on participant turnout, and each experiment had three rounds.

Off-the-shelf LLMs, while shown to be persuasive \cite{breum2024persuasive}, are not personalized. Therefore, we design the personalized LLM bot such that given a statement and its factuality, it can personalize the argument considering individual’s preferred news sources, and rhetorical style (see SM, Section \ref{exp_llm_design_supp}, \ref{tablearticles}, \ref{tab:llmsamples1}, \ref{tab:llmsamples2}, \ref{tab:llmsamples3}, and \ref{tab:llmsamples4}). Using GPT-4o-mini as the base LLM model, this is done in three distinct stages. First, given information about the user, a traditional machine learning model predicts individuals’ preferred news sources and rhetorical style. Next, an external database, containing over 70,000 full-length articles, is queried for articles pertaining the statement. We specifically focused on 10 news sources, balancing representation from left, right, and center ideological leanings. The model then performs a summarization step, prompted to pull in relevant information from the resulting query. Finally, the model is instructed to reframe the summarized information to incorporate the predicted rhetorical style. 


\subsection*{Results}

\subsubsection*{Personalized LLM Responses Shift Beliefs Toward Factual Accuracy}


Belief shift was computed by centering each participant’s response score around the veracity label (e.g., true or false) and measuring the signed change in their updated rating, where a negative shift implies a shift towards the accuracy (see SM Section \ref{evaluation_metrics}). We find that participants who received personalized responses from the LLM bot were significantly more likely to update their beliefs in the direction of factual accuracy, compared to those in the control condition. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:beliefupdate} (Panels A and B) and Table~\ref{tab:overallshift}, the average belief shift was significantly greater in the treatment group as a result of the bot's presence, with an average shift of -0.35 in the treatment and -0.1 in the control ($p < 0.0001$; see SM Section \ref{robustness_supp} and Figure~\ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason}). This pattern held across statement factuality, salience, economic relevance, and self-reported media skepticism (see SM Section \ref{studylevel}, Figures~\ref{fig:finding3_split_truevfalse} - \ref{fig:finding3_split_newstrust}, and Tables~\ref{tab:robustness} and \ref{tab:ttesttrustsome}). It also held across data collection periods (pre-election vs. post-election; see SM Section \ref{prepost}, Figures~\ref{fig:alldist_supplementals} - \ref{fig:case_poltrust}, and Tables~\ref{tab:controlpvp} - \ref{tab:caseproofofinsig}), and demographic groups (see SM Sections \ref{belief_demographic} and \ref{belief_demographic_regress}, Figures~\ref{fig:misinfo_diff_age} - \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_pol_strength}, and Tables~ \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_education} - \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_pol_strength}, Tables~\ref{tab:misinfo_diff_control_reg} and \ref{tab:misinfo_diff_case_reg} for regressions). This is consistent with hypothesis 1.

Self-reported outcomes from the post-survey after completing the experiment further supported the intervention's effect. Participants in the treatment group were more likely to say they changed their mind about any of the statements (Figure~\ref{fig:beliefupdate}, Panel C; $p < 0.05$) and more likely to report feeling better informed after the experiment compared to those in the control (Panel D; $p < 0.001$; see SM Table~\ref{tab:proportiontestsmain} for proportion test results). Our findings were consistent across both time-frames (see SM Section \ref{prepost}, Figures~\ref{fig:cont_proportions} and \ref{fig:case_proportions}, and Tables~\ref{tab:controlproofpropinsig} and \ref{tab:caseproofpropinsig}). These results suggest that personalized LLM messaging influenced belief revision as well as  participants’ confidence about being informed.


%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%START HERE%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\subsubsection*{Participants Follow the Bot and Seek Out Others Aligned with Its Beliefs}

The LLM intervention influenced the structure of participants’ social networks. Consistent with hypothesis 2a, the majority of participants in the treatment condition (70.2\%) chose to follow the bot at least once, and over half of these individuals (54.4\%) continued following it for all three rounds of the study (Figure~\ref{fig:networkupdate}, Panel A; see SM Sections \ref{regress_botfol} and \ref{prop_botfol}, Figures ~\ref{fig:follow_age} - \ref{fig:follow_pol_strength} and Table~\ref{tab:multilinear_reg} suggesting no significant difference in results between demographic groups). While the effect of the bot is prevalent throughout the treatment condition results, the use of personal pronouns by participants in their responses and a mix of source-leaning cues by the bot responses lead to stronger shifts (see SM Section \ref{persuasivellm} and Figures~\ref{fig:botpersuasion_personal} and \ref{fig:botpersuasion_sourcelean}). We also find that participants who follow the bot in stage 3 tend to shift their beliefs closer to the truth in stage 2 (see SM Section \ref{botfolvchange}). This suggests that participants did not treat the bot as a one-off novelty, but rather as a sustained source of potential guidance within the evolving network.


Beyond the bot itself, participants tended to follow human peers whose views were more closely aligned with the bot’s accurate stance, as predicted by hypothesis 2b. While both groups engage in truth-seeking behaviors \cite{pennycook2021shifting, bond2023engagement} (see SM Section \ref{networklevel} and Figure \ref{fig:botfollowvrandomtruth}), we find individuals in the treatment experience this truth pursuit more dramatically than those in the control. To quantify this tendency, we computed a ``follow signal'' for each participant: the mean factual accuracy score (calibrated by truth direction) of the individuals they chose to follow at each round, averaged over all three rounds. The score was normalized such that responses closer to the truth yielded lower values, and the most truthful individual---either the bot, if followed, or the lowest-scoring peer---was excluded to enable fair comparisons (see SM Section \ref{evaluation_metrics} and Equation~\ref{eq:followsig}). The average follow signal was significantly lower in the treatment condition (1.55) than in the control (2.02; $p < 0.0001$), as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:networkupdate}, Panel B and Table~\ref{tab:followsignal}. Given the adjusted belief scale ranges from 0 (most accurate option) to 4 (least accurate option), our results suggest that participants in the treatment notably shift towards more truthful network compositions. Moreover, we find that networks became more assortative between stages 2 and 3 (see SM Section \ref{networklevel} and Figures~\ref{fig:assortativity_control} and \ref{fig:assortativity_case}), which implies individuals are not simply choosing who they follow at random. Thus, the presence of the bot had downstream consequences in shaping individuals’ subsequent social networks --- here toward more accurate information.

Importantly, participants were not unaware of the bot's presence. In the post-surveys, 51\% of treatment participants reported interacting with a bot, compared to 22\% in the control group (Figure~\ref{fig:networkupdate}, Panel C). Despite this recognition, the bot remained influential \cite{matz2024potential}. Participants in the treatment adopted similar beliefs and social connections, including following the bot, suggesting that perceived artificiality did not undermine trust or effectiveness \cite{matz2024potential}. This persistence of influence, even under partial awareness, reinforces the robustness of the intervention's social effects.


\subsection*{Discussion}
We show that personalized LLM interventions can support belief updates toward ground truth in the context of political statements. The fact that participants followed the bot at high rates and sought out others aligned with its position indicates that targeted AI agents can influence both individual cognition and network-level structure. Individuals tend to seek truth \cite{pennycook2021shifting}, and by embedding a truthful agent within the social context, our intervention amplified this baseline tendency. We find no difference in the efficacy of the intervention across multiple factors, including the statement veracity, economic relevance, topic salience, individual demographic traits, and time of data collection. This suggests that the intervention is robust. 

To our knowledge, this is the first study to empirically demonstrate that a personalized LLM embedded in a social network can reshape the surrounding social topology in a direction aligned with factual accuracy. Participants in the treatment condition were more likely to connect with others whose views were closer to the ground truth, compared to those in the control group. These findings point to the dual function of such agents: they serve as direct informants and as catalysts for reconfiguring information flows in a network. In contemporary online ecosystems, where individuals are routinely exposed to conflicting signals, personalized LLMs may offer a scalable way to redirect attention toward reliable sources and re-anchor belief trajectories.

Notably, the observed belief shifts occurred even without a back-and-forth dialogue and even when participants were not explicitly aware that they were interacting with a bot (note that they were made aware that a bot might be present and had provided consent to interacting with one). These features make our experimental setup more reflective of actual digital environments, where users often engage with brief messages and may only have partial awareness of whether content is AI-generated. 



At the same time, the mechanisms that enable this influence also carry clear risks. Prior studies have shown that users often accept LLM responses, even when they are factually incorrect or deliberately misleading \cite{sharma2024would, deverna2024fact}. Our results underscore how even modest personalization and contextual awareness can enhance credibility. Thus, replacing our guardrails with maligned structures makes it plausible that a similarly structured but malicious bot could amplify misinformation rather than mitigate it. As LLM-driven systems become more integrated into public discourse, designing effective guardrails such as transparent sourcing, regular audits, and limits on persuasive framing will be essential. Our findings help define what such systems can do and where oversight must be targeted. The results make clear that LLMs have enormous potential in not only altering beliefs but also altering the very social fabric in which people interact. 

As moderating content on large-scale social media platforms becomes more difficult to complete directly, personalized LLMs could be utilized as a potential method. With user permission, individuals could receive persuasive, factual responses to potential sources of misinformed beliefs in any information domain. To ensure responsible use, not only should guardrails as we describe here be considered, but also be extended to further protect users and incorporate auditing, such as receiving consent and not collecting any personally identifiable information. Such personalized content should focus on ensuring transparency, fairness, and accountability in how the system operates -- positioning them as assistive technologies for navigating today’s complex information environment.


This work can shape future research within the space of personalized LLMs and factors of belief. For example, conducting a similar study within other information environments would help reinforce the generalization of these findings. Furthermore, investigating the effects of such an intervention in real-world platforms would shed light on its efficacy in a setting with more complex information streams. While considerable research addresses how LLMs affect beliefs, our results accentuate that the impact may go further by altering the social networks within which we exchange information. Thus, it is imperative to continue to study LLM interactions within social settings consisting of both human and AI interactions, and to protect the end users throughout the process.

\section*{Materials and Methods}
\label{methods}
We are interested in how personalized information from an LLM bot (relative to the absence of a personalized bot) impacts beliefs and subsequent social network construction. The basic structure of the study placed individuals in a social network and then had them: 1) report their belief about the veracity of a statement and explain their rationale with brief text, 2) learn about the veracity judgments of others in the social network, 3) have the opportunity to update their belief and explain it again, and, 4) choose whom from the network they would like to follow. We made two additional design decisions. First, we followed prior political science work on opinion formation by including four entities in a social network \cite{klar2014partisanship, druckman2018no}. Participants in each network took part concurrently (and were recruited to do so). There was a median of 16 participants per study batch, within the range 10-28 participants. This variation is due in some part to the timing in the day of the experiment and participant availability. Framework limitations also play a role, such as 10 participants being required to participate in order for the experiment to work properly, and a maximum of 24 people can be supported in the treatment because of time constraints on bot response generation. Second, we created a dynamic setting where individuals took part in three rounds (with each proceeding as described below). A choice in one round influenced later rounds. Specifically, when a participant chose someone to follow in an earlier round, that actor became more likely to appear in the participant’s subsequent round(s) of the social networks. This increased experimental realism, which refers to the extent to which participants take the study seriously \cite{druckman2022experimental}. Making consequential choices presumably increases engagement.

For reference, see Figures \ref{fig:stage1}, \ref{fig:stage2}, \ref{fig:stage3} to view the interface for all parts of the experiment, which are described below. Note that while these figures depict real responses from participants and a bot, this does not reflect a real snapshot of one round of a given experiment; the figures are purely for framework description. While the interfaces remain consistent across all rounds, the behavior in round 1 differs slightly from rounds 2 and 3.

The precise sequence for the \textbf{first round} was as follows.

\subsection*{\textbf{Stage 1: Response stage (First round)}}
Participants are provided with a prompt statement on one of the following topics: immigration, inflation, fuel and oil, or overpopulation. Some of these statements were true while others were false. More details on how these statements were selected are provided in section \ref{PoliticalStatement} of Supplemental Materials. Participants reported how much they believed the statement to be true on a 5-point scale (with higher scores indicating stronger belief that the statement is true). They additionally provided reasoning for their rating in a maximum of 1,000 characters. We refer to each evaluation and its accompanying explanation as a ``response entry.'' All participants in a given network receive the same statement. 

\subsection*{\textbf{Stage 2: Revision stage (First round)}}
In the revision stage, participants received the response entries of a few others in the network. Participants re-rated the same prompt again on a 5-point scale, and also selected from a pre-determined list of reasons the rationale behind their selection (see Supplement Section \ref{selfreportbeliefupdate} for options). The participant's initial rating is displayed to ensure that any change in their rating is intentional. However, even if they do not change their response, participants still had to click the scale manually. 

This stage includes our experimental manipulation. In the control, participants were shown the entries of three other participants in the study. In the treatment, participants viewed the entries of two other participants as well as that of the personalized bot. The personalized LLM bot always provided the correct value, with a response entry tailored to the participant’s preference. 

\subsection*{\textbf{Stage 3: Selection stage (First round)}}
In the selection stage, participants were presented with six response entries. Participants learned these entries came from those they previously followed, and/or those `recommended' by the system. Participants saw the three peers from stage 2 (including the bot for the treatment condition), with the other three being randomly recommended. This setup ensures that participants get access to diverse responses. The only difference in the selection stage between control and the treatment is that in the treatment, one of the response entries is that of the personalized bot. 

Participants must then like or dislike each response entry (to prompt thoughtful engagement with the content) and select (i.e., ``followed") three peers whose answers they would like to subsequently see in the next round. They could stick to the peers assigned at stage 2 or pick new ones (or do a mix of both). Through this stage, we can evaluate how participants restructured their networks, including whether they chose to follow the personalized bot and incorporate the bot into their networks. We can also quantify the changes in the participants' networks given the presence of the bot. 

\vspace{2em}
\noindent

\textbf{Rounds 2 and 3} were similar, with a few changes to account for increasing experimental realism. Participants have the same stage 1 but with a new prompt on the same topic (i.e., a new statement on the same issue). Stages 2 and 3 for rounds 2 and 3) differed, however, as follows. 

\subsection*{\textbf{Stage 2: Revision stage}}
Similar to round 1, participants saw three others. For the control, there was one randomly chosen person that they had followed in the prior round and two others they had not followed (randomly chosen). For the treatment, the participants saw the personalized bot, a followed human participant (chosen at random), and a non-followed human participant (chosen at random). As mentioned, we ensured participants saw at least one person they had followed to provide them with partial autonomy over their networks (and thus, their social influence). We included non-followed individuals to minimize the possibility of extreme homophily. 

\subsection*{\textbf{Stage 3: Selection stage}}
In stage 3, participants saw the peers they were shown in stage 2 (including the bot for the treatment condition), those they followed in the previous round, and the rest were randomly recommended. This ensures that the setup maintains the ``social media" structure, where once someone follows a person, they do not get unfollowed unless the user manually unfollows them. 

\subsection*{\textbf{Pre and Post Survey}}

After users provide their consent to be a part of the study, we collect a few demographic and personality measures. For gathering demographic data, we used the categories as used in previous literature \cite{proma2024exploring}. For measuring personality, we utilized shortened ``big 5'' personality trait questionnaire which contained 10 questions \cite{rammstedt2007measuring}. This provides the basis for our personalized LLM and allows us to check demographic differences in behavior. Upon entering the study, the users provide the following information:

\begin{itemize}
    \item Username
    \item ProlificID
    \item Age (18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-54, 65+)
    \item Gender (Male, Female, Non-binary, Prefer not to answer)
    \item Race (White, Hispanic, Black or African American, Asian, American Indian or Alaska Native, Other)
    \item Education level (High school diploma, Associate degree, Bachelor's degree, Graduate or professional degree, Other)
    \item Political Party (Democratic, Republican, Independent, Other)
    \item Strength of Political Identification (Very weak, Somewhat weak, Neutral, Somewhat strong, Very strong)
    \item Location (State)
    \item Occupation
    \item Extroversion
    \item Agreeableness
    \item Conscientiousness
    \item Neuroticism
    \item Openness
\end{itemize}

Upon completing all three rounds of the study, users then fill out a post survey survey, which includes the following questions (those bolded considered for analysis within the manuscript):

\begin{itemize}
    \item How often do you get your news from social media?
    \item Please identify which social media platforms you get your news from: (check all that apply)
    \item Please identity which news sources you generally trust: (check all that apply)
    \item Which of the following information characteristics do you consider when determining its factuality? (check all that apply)
    \item Which of the following personal characteristics have an impact when determining information factuality? (check all that apply)
    \item \textbf{Did going through the experiment change your mind about any statements?}
    \item \textbf{Do you feel more informed about the political topics shown after going through the experiment?}
    \item \textbf{How do you feel about political news at this current point in time?}
    \item When considering the responses of others, how relevant were any sources they cited in your decision making?
    \item When considering the responses of others, how relevant was the logic of their statement in your decision making?
    \item When considering the responses of others, how relevant was the emotion of their statement in your decision making?
    \item \textbf{At any point of the experiment, did you feel like you were interacting with bots instead of real participants?}
    \item Please provide your feedback on the experience. This can include any problems you encountered or any other issues you faced during the experiment.
\end{itemize}

Upon submitting the post survey, participants were then debriefed regarding statement factuality and the potential for bot engagement during the study (note that participants were previously told that there may or may not be a bot present). They were also provided with contact information of the researchers in the treatment they had further questions. 


\section{Evaluation Metrics}
\label{evaluation_metrics}

To generate all shift plots (i.e., plots showing shift towards or away from the truth),  we first encoded the initial and updated scores as a value from [0, 4], where 0 represents ``Strongly Disbelieve'' and 4 represents ``Strongly Believe,'' since these were the labels provided to participants during the study. To account for the distinction between true and false statements,  the difference between the two values for statements with the ground truth of ``true'' are calculated as initial - updated, and statements with the ground truth ``false'' are calculated as updated - initial. These calculations ensure that a shift in the intended direction is encoded as a negative change, while a shift towards misinformed beliefs is encoded as a positive change. For each person, this difference was averaged over all rounds, and then plotted using a kernel density plot. For determining distribution differences, all calculations use the t-score to calculate the confidence interval and p-value. When confidence intervals between findings of interest overlap, Levene’s test is utilized to determine whether the variance between the two samples are equivalent, then the appropriate t-test is conducted based on those results to determine significance. Levene’s test is considered to be a robust test \cite{Boos_Bartlett_Boos_Box_Brown_Brown_Conover_Draper_Geng_1999} utilized in prior works \cite{Sun_Zhou_Hauptschein_Rappoport_Xu_Navarro}. We use t-tests because the standard deviation of the underlying population is not known, and initial tests indicate the distribution was not normal.

For calculating the follow signal, we consider the subset of individuals within a given round that were followed by each participant. For each person's followed subset, we drop the most truthful person when 3 people were followed (which is mostly the case, except for a few edge cases). We then average the scores of the followed participants, again normalized to true/false statements by considering the initial score in the false case and 4 - initial score in the true case for all followed players. This ensures a score of 0 is the most truthful score. After computing the average follow signal for each round, we then find the mean across all rounds; this represents the average follow signal across the whole experiment for a given individual (see Equation \ref{eq:followsig}). This is again plotted using a kernel density plot and tested for significance in a similar procedure as described for shift evaluations.

\begin{equation}
    \delta_{follow signal} = \frac{\sum^3_{i = 1} \frac{(\sum^n_{j = 1} f_j) - f_{min}}{n-1}}{3}
    \label{eq:followsig}
\end{equation}

When computing proportions, we take the number of participants who fall into a specified category and divide it by the sum of all answers given. To compare proportions, we utilize a two proportion z test, where we compare the proportion of the given category across two conditions.



\section{Designing the Experiment and the Personalized LLM Bot}
\label{exp_llm_design_supp}
Below describes our specific processes for determining elements of experiment design and the personalized LLM bot.

\subsection{Experimental Design}
\label{exp_design_supp}

Beyond the experimental platform design, other aspects of the design had to be considered: the news sources the LLM bot should be able to access, the political statements individuals would see during the experiment, and the selection of our time-frames for hosting these studies. Each of these is discussed in detail below.

\subsubsection{Selection of the news sources}
\label{news_sources}
The news sources an individual chooses to trust can be affected by a variety of factors, and as a result, our goal was to select a wide variety of news sources that would encapsulate the potentially diverse opinions/preferences of individuals. Several resources were consulted and compared to create a comprehensive, representative list of trustworthy sources. One of the most important factors for trust in news sources is political affiliation. According to a 2020 report from Pew Research Center \cite{jurkowitz2020democrats}, a large proportion of U.S. adults trust sources such as CNN, CBS, and Fox News. Similarly, a Cooperative Election Study (CES) Common Content 2022 study conducted ``across a nationally representative sample of 60,000 American adults" which showed that Americans engage with several news networks, including CNN, MSNBC, and Fox News \cite{schaffner2021cooperative}. Next, we considered AllSides Media Bias Chart and ``The Chart" created by Ad Fontes in 2018 \cite{harvardResearchGuides} to determine the political leaning and the factuality of the sources. The factuality and leaning of these sources were cross-referenced with those provided by ground.news \cite{GroundNews}, a website that also provides media bias and factuality ratings aggregated according to the news reported by a news source. Through this process, we shortlist potential news sources, ensuring a relatively equal representation of left, right, and central sources. Next, we checked whether their API is publicly available through GNews and if enough articles can be extracted from that source to build our RAG. Our final set of 10 news sources were Washington Examiner (right), New York Post (right), Fox News (right), AP News (center), The Economist (center), BBC (center), New York Times (left), CNN (left), Washington Post (left), and MSNBC (left). Note that the news preference dataset was built considering these 10 news sources, and the articles from these news sources were used to build our RAG. The number of articles extracted from each source is provided in Table \ref{tablearticles}. 


\subsubsection{Political Statement Generation}
\label{PoliticalStatement}
We selected four specific topics --- overpopulation, inflation, immigration, and fuel and oil --- of varying saliency levels, to ensure generalizability of our experimental setup. The topics were selected based on reported saliency of issues during the period of the 2024 US presidential election, balancing with two high salience (inflation and immigration) and two low salience (overpopulation and fuel and oil) topics \cite{gallup, Jones_2025}. We curate a series of political statements for each of the topics. These statements must be bipartisan and with objective ground truth. The statements themselves can be true or false. To ensure a variety of statements, we generate them in two different ways. First, we conduct a series of in-person focus group studies, where participants come up with their own politics-related statements, and find their corresponding verifying information online. This provided insights into the personal aspects of misinformation (i.e., what makes statements believable for individuals). To create the statements used for this study, we relied on credible information to prove or disprove our statements from government published statistics, Politifact, FactCheck.org and Gallup. The final selected statements are provided in Tables \ref{statements_part1}, \ref{statements_part2}, and \ref{statements_part3}. 

% All the participants are shown the statements and the corresponding verifying information generated, through a majority voting system, the top ones are selected to be included. Second, we look through online sources such as Politifact, AP News (specifically, a column called Not Real News) and FactCheck.org to find the most popular topics and corresponding verifying information. 

\subsubsection{Selection of our time-frames}
\label{timeframe}
We conducted our study before and after elections. The duration for before elections was October 1 - October 31, 2024 and after the elections, it was November 15 - December 15, 2024. There are prior work suggesting that there is some change in beliefs pre and post elections \cite{banducci2003elections}. However, we did not have prior predictions about it moderating the treatment effects. Our results show that the differences in context do not, in fact, affect the effectiveness of the intervention. More details about these results are presented in Section \ref{prepost}.

% However, to our knowledge, there are no prior predictions about it moderating the treatment effects. Rather, our selected time frames were chosen to see if the results are robust and generalizable across contexts. We argue that pre-election and post-election contexts are different since there is a clear ``winner" and a clear ``loser" of the elections, which can affect individual perceptions \cite{fasching2024persistent, banducci2003elections}. Moreover, various studies have also shown that elections act as a short-term polarizing event, with partisan identities becoming less salient after the elections, further contributing to the fact that the context between pre and post elections are different \cite{michelitch2018electoral}.

\subsection{Personalized LLM Bot}
\label{personalizedllmbot}
Our goal was to first design an LLM bot that can incorporate an individual's preferred news sources and rhetorical styling to create compelling arguments. The personalized bot design follows a four-step pipeline to generate the responses using ChatGPT as the base model. At first, we predict users' news source preferences and their preferred rhetorical style from ethos, pathos, and logos using K-Means clustering and collaborative filtering. The preferred news source predictions are then passed to the RAG model. The RAG contains news articles from 2023 to 2024 from the 10 sources previously mentioned in section \ref{news_sources}. The model finds related articles, considering the predicted news source preference, and then summarizes those articles to 3-4 sentences. The exact prompts used are provided below. This summarized information, along with the predicted rhetorical style, is then passed to another LLM, which rephrases the summarized information to incorporate the rhetorical style provided. We provide tables that capture a variety of LLM bot final outputs, along with their initial input statement (Tables \ref{tab:llmsamples1},\ref{tab:llmsamples2}, \ref{tab:llmsamples3},\ref{tab:llmsamples4}). For anonymity, the demographics and personality input into the system are not given. The table shows the different variations in facts, sources, and styles the LLM utilized.

\subsubsection{Summarization Generation Prompts}

\textbf{True Statement Condition}: Given that the `Information' is true, summarize the relevant facts of each of the `Excerpts' that support the `Information'. Keep the source for each of the `Excerpts' in the summary. After summarizing, remove all summaries not relevant to `Information'. Do not use any hate speech or vulgar language.

\noindent
\textbf{False Statement Condition}: Given that the `Information' is false, summarize the relevant facts of each of the `Excerpts' that disprove the `Information'. Keep the source for each of the `Excerpts' in the summary. After summarizing, remove all summaries not relevant to `Information'. Do not use any hate speech or vulgar language.

\subsubsection{Rhetorical Styling Prompts}
\textbf{True Statement Condition}: You are an informed citizen, persuading another citizen that the `Information' is true. Read the `Summary' and identify relevant facts. Then, write a first person response to prove the `Information' by \textit{$<$best tactic here$>$}. Do not use hate speech or vulgar language. Limit the response to 4 sentences.

\noindent
\textbf{False Statement Condition}: You are an informed citizen, persuading another citizen that the `Information' is false. Read the `Summary' and identify relevant facts. Then, write a first person response to disprove the `Information' by \textit{$<$best tactic here$>$}. Do not use hate speech or vulgar language. Limit the response to 4 sentences. 

\textbf{Ethos Tactic}: emphasizing the credibility of the news sources.

\textbf{Pathos Tactic}: emphasizing empathy towards the reader

\section{Robustness Measures}
\label{robustness_supp}

\subsection{Participant Demographics}
\label{part_demographics}
Table \ref{tab:participant_dem} shows the demographic breakdown of participants in the treatment and control groups. The distributions for control and the treatment are matched in terms of age range, gender, race, political affiliation, and all five personality traits (see Table \ref{tab:chi2_demographics}, \ref{tab:mwu_personality}). 

\subsection{Belief Shift Across Demographic Differences}
\label{belief_demographic}
To further prove robustness of the interventions, we evaluate differences in demographics across participants. We compare average shift (calibrated for true/false statements) for each person, and we find no significant difference within group across any demographics, except for age range in the treatment. Note that older population has been previously shown to be less flexible compared to younger population \cite{wilson2018age}. The plots are shown in Figures \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_age}, \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_race}, \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_education}, \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_gender}, \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_pol}, and \ref{fig:misinfo_diff_pol_strength}. The within analysis using ANOVA are shown in \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_age_range}, \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_race}, \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_education}, \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_gender}, \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_political}, and \ref{tab:within_group_analysis_pol_strength}. The between analysis are shown in Tables \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_age_range}, \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_gender}, \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_political}, \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_pol_strength}, 
\ref{tab:between_group_analysis_race}, and \ref{tab:between_group_analysis_education}. 

\subsection{Regression of Belief Shift Across Demographic and Personality Differences}
\label{belief_demographic_regress}
We use a multiple linear regression model using Strata to model whether there are demography and personality-based differences in if individuals move towards the truth or not in the treatment and the control. All features were not significant in the treatment, except for age range. None of the features in control were significant. Overall, our results suggest that the effect was similar across all individuals. The results are shown in Tables \ref{tab:misinfo_diff_control_reg} and \ref{tab:misinfo_diff_case_reg}. 

\subsection{Regression of Bot Following Across Demographic and Personality Differences}
\label{regress_botfol}
We use a multiple linear regression model using Strata to model demography and personality-based differences in whether an individual follows the bot. Our results suggest that older individuals (p = 0.001) are less likely to follow the bot. The rest were not statistically significant. All results are shown in Table \ref{tab:multilinear_reg}. 

\subsection{Proportion of Bot Following Across Demographic and Personality Differences}
\label{prop_botfol}
We conduct chi-square tests for demographics to see if there is any connection between who individuals follow and their demographics, complementing the regression model. We find that there is no significance difference based on age range (Chi-square = 20.426, p-value = 0.0594, dof = 12), education level (Chi-square = 9.200, p-value = 0.4190, dof = 9), gender (Chi-square = 6.228, p-value = 0.1010, dof = 3), race (Chi-square = 10.287, p-value = 0.3277, dof = 9), political affiliation (Chi-square = 6.513, p-value = 0.3682, dof = 6), and political strength (Chi-square = 18.248, p-value = 0.1084, dof = 12). The plots are in Figures \ref{fig:follow_age}, \ref{fig:follow_education}, \ref{fig:follow_gender}, \ref{fig:follow_race}, \ref{fig:follow_political}, \ref{fig:follow_pol_strength}. 


\subsection{Pre-Election and Post-Election Checks of Differences}
\label{prepost}

Because data collection occurred before and after the election, we tested to identify differences in results between the treatment and control. We find no evidence of significantly diverging findings between the two periods (as shown in Supplemental figures). Thus, both samples were combined for the main paper results. The results splitting ``Pre-Election'' and ``Post-Election'',  are provided in Supplemental Figures \ref{fig:alldist_supplementals}, \ref{fig:cont_proportions}, \ref{fig:case_proportions}, \ref{fig:bot_follow}, \ref{fig:followsignal}, \ref{fig:cont_groundtruth}, \ref{fig:case_groundtruth}, \ref{fig:cont_salience}, \ref{fig:case_salience}, \ref{fig:cont_econ}, \ref{fig:case_econ}, \ref{fig:cont_poltrust}, and \ref{fig:case_poltrust}, and in Supplemental Tables \ref{tab:controlpvp}, \ref{tab:caseproofofinsig}, \ref{tab:casepvp}, \ref{tab:controlproofofinsig}, \ref{tab:caseproofofinsig}, \ref{tab:controlproofpropinsig}, and \ref{tab:caseproofpropinsig}.

\subsection{Study-Level Differences}
\label{studylevel}
We empirically evaluate the efficacy of the intervention across the veracity of the statements (true/false), saliency levels of the topic, economic relevancy of the topic, and the reported skepticism in political news (see Figures~\ref{fig:finding3_split_truevfalse}, \ref{fig:finding3_split_salience}, \ref{fig:finding3_split_salience}, and \ref{fig:finding3_split_newstrust} and Table \ref{tab:robustness}). We find that across all measures, the treatment significantly moves closer to the truth than the control. The only exception to this phenomenon was for responses to ``Trust all political news'' (which 0 participants selected) and ``Trust some political news'' (which few participants selected, leading to poor statistical power), where the difference was insignificant. 

\subsection{Self-Reported Belief Updates}
\label{selfreportbeliefupdate}
Within the experiments, at stage 2, participants are asked to select reasons as to why they are updating their opinion, which include options such as the following:

\begin{itemize}
    \item ``I did not change my mind'' (abbreviated to ``No change'' in Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason})
    \item ``The believability ratings of my peers changed my mind'' (abbreviated to ``Peer ratings'' in Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason})
    \item ``I thought about the topic more on my own'' (abbreviated to ``Thought'' in Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason})
    \item ``The reasons stated in the answer of my peers changed my mind'' (abbreviated to ``Peer reason'' in Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason})
    \item ``I found new information from other sources not related to this experiment (eg. social media, news, friends and family)'' (abbreviated to ``New information'' in Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason})
    \item ``Other''
\end{itemize}

From Figure \ref{fig:stage2_beliefupdatereason}, we find that individuals in the treatment selected ``No change'' less frequently than the control, and ``Peer ratings'', ``peer reasoning'', and ``new information'' more often than the control. We attribute the significance of the ``Peer ratings'' and ``peer reasoning'' to the presence of the bot, as this is the only difference between the treatment and control in stage 2. While it is unclear what ``new information'' could refer to, it could also be interpreted as individuals feeling moved by the facts and sources cited by the bot.


\subsection{The connection between changing rating and following the bot}
\label{botfolvchange}
To understand if there is a connection between individual rating and following the bot, we take a more granular look at the treatment group. For each round for each participant, we consider if they followed the bot or not, and calculate their belief change (with a more negative rating meaning moving closer to the truth). Our results show that the mean change in rating was almost twice as high when they followed the bot compared to when they did not follow the bot. Mean change was -0.473 (CI: -0.526, -0.419) for when they followed the bot, and mean was -0.210 (CI: -0.261, -0.159), when they did not follow the bot. This is consistent with the possibility that the individuals altered their beliefs due to the bot, and then chose to follow the bot. We cannot, however, directly test that dynamic since we cannot isolate the precise actor in the network that influenced a respondent’s beliefs. 


\subsection{Network-Level Following Trends}
\label{networklevel}
Given the main paper focuses on effects at the individual level, we also look at network effects. First, we examine the assortativity of the network, or how often individuals connect with others of similar beliefs. We find that individuals move towards homophily. This analysis is done by comparing stage 2 and stage 3, since individuals have a choice in stage 3 but not in stage 2 (all stage 2 and stage 3 differences significant at p \textless 0.001). We highlight these findings to show that individuals in both conditions are not updating their preferences at random. 

Since individuals in both the treatment and control are not updating their following at random, we then investigate how often individuals follow the bot per round, compared with how often individuals follow the ``most truthful'' option in control. When there is potentially more than one ``most truthful'' option (for example, two people have the same value), we select one from the set at random and check whether the individual followed them. This is meant to be comparable to the bot follow in the treatment, since the bot can be considered as only one ``user". Here we see similar trends in following these individuals between the treatment and the control (p = 0.118), suggesting that individuals in both the treatment and the control tend to pursue others with more truthful beliefs.

% We also look into the assortativity of the network, or how often individuals connect with others of similar beliefs. We find that individuals move towards homophily. This analysis is done by comparing stage 2 and stage 3, since individuals have a choice in stage 3 but not in stage 2 (all stage 2 and stage 3 differences significant at p \textless 0.001). We highlight these findings to show that individuals in both conditions are not updating their preferences at random, but rather are updating their networks towards the truth, and argue this pursuit of truth can be leveraged for supporting LLM interventions such as ours in the future. 

These findings in tandem show that the individuals within the experiment are utilizing the follow mechanic as intended, and individuals pursue truth within their networks. The plots are in Figures \ref{fig:botfollowvrandomtruth}, \ref{fig:assortativity_control} and \ref{fig:assortativity_case}. We argue this pursuit of truth can be leveraged for supporting LLM interventions such as ours in the future. 

\subsection{Persuasiveness of the LLM Bot}
\label{persuasivellm}
All previous work discussed in this manuscript points to the implication that our LLM intervention is, in fact, persuasive. Prior works have emphasized that LLMs can embody persuasive traits \cite{costello2024durably, breum2024persuasive, Argyle_Busby_Gubler_Lyman_Olcott_Pond_Wingate_2025}. That being said, we are interested in understanding why our LLM intervention is persuasive. In order to identify what aspects of the intervention make it persuasive, we analyzed message properties from Stage 1 for both the participants and the LLM intervention, comparing the shifts. We find that personal references within participant responses and displaying a mix of partisan cues through source references (compared to one partisan cue) were significant. 

Figure \ref{fig:botpersuasion_personal} shows the results of the control and treatment shifts, partitioned on whether or not the participant utilized personal pronouns within their Stage 1 written response. Personal pronouns include ``I'', ``we'', ``our'', ``us'', and variants of those including contractions. ``us'' was explicitly checked for whether or not it was referring to ``US'' (United States) since many of our statements are about the US at large. We find no notable difference in the control conditions (p = 0.179), while the treatment condition shows a larger shift when individuals reference personal pronouns (p \textless 0.00001). Given this is only significant in the treatment, this suggests that the bot has more of an influence on individuals who feel the topic is personally relevant, which aligns with prior persuasion work \cite{Luttrell_2018, Petty_Krosnick_2014}.

Figure \ref{fig:botpersuasion_sourcelean} shows the results of the treatment shifts, partitioned on whether the LLM intervention pulled in sources of a single political leaning compared against when it showed sources of different political leanings. The results show that individuals shifted more towards the truth when a variety of source leanings is provided (p \textless 0.05), though this happens somewhat infrequently throughout the experiments (n = 241 where individuals saw a mix of political leanings in sources in a given round, n = 962 where individuals saw one political leaning cue in a given round). This suggests that pulling in cross-partisan agreement can boost persuasiveness by mitigating partisan motivated reasoning, as shown in prior works \cite{Bolsen_Druckman_Cook_2014, druckman2003framing}.

title: GigaAM: Efficient Self-Supervised Learner for Speech Recognition
summary:
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has demonstrated strong performance in speech
processing, particularly in automatic speech recognition. In this paper, we
explore an SSL pretraining framework that leverages masked language modeling
with targets derived from a speech recognition model. We also present chunkwise
attention with dynamic chunk size sampling during pretraining to enable both
full-context and streaming fine-tuning. Our experiments examine scaling with
respect to model size and the amount of data. Using our method, we train the
GigaAM family of models, including a state-of-the-art model for Russian speech
recognition that outperforms Whisper-large-v3 by 50%. We have released our
foundation and ASR models, along with the inference code, under the MIT license
as open-source resources to the research community. Available at
https://github.com/salute-developers/gigaam.

bib.abstract: The Common Voice corpus is a massively-multilingual collection of transcribed speech intended for speech technology research and development. Common Voice is designed for Automatic Speech Recognition purposes but can be useful in other domains (e.g. language identification). To achieve scale and sustainability, the Common Voice project employs crowdsourcing for both data collection and data validation. The most recent release includes 29 languages, and as of November 2019 there are a total of 38 languages collecting data. Over 50,000 individuals have participated so far, resulting in 2,500 hours of collected audio. To our knowledge this is the largest audio corpus in the public domain for speech recognition, both in terms of number of hours and number of languages. As an example use case for Common Voice, we present speech recognition experiments using MozillaвЂ™s DeepSpeech Speech-to-Text toolkit. By applying transfer learning from a source English model, we find an average Character Error Rate improvement of 5.99 В± 5.48 for twelve target languages (German, French, Italian, Turkish, Catalan, Slovenian, Welsh, Irish, Breton, Tatar, Chuvash, and Kabyle). For most of these languages, these are the first ever published results on end-to-end Automatic Speech Recognition.

bib.abstract: We investigate the optimal model size and number of tokens for training a Transformer language model under a given compute budget. We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant. By training over 400 language models ranging from 70 million to over 16 billion parameters on 5 to 500 billion tokens, we find that for compute-optimal training, the model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled equally: for every doubling of model size the number of training tokens should also be doubled. We test this hypothesis by training a predicted compute-optimal model, Chinchilla, that uses the same compute budget as Gopher but with 70B parameters and 4\texttimes{} more more data. Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperforms Gopher (280B), GPT-3 (175B), Jurassic-1 (178B), and Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) on a large range of downstream evaluation tasks. This also means that Chinchilla uses substantially less compute for fine-tuning and inference, greatly facilitating downstream usage. As a highlight, Chinchilla reaches a state-of-the-art average accuracy of 67.5\% on the MMLU benchmark, greater than a 7\% improvement over Gopher.

bib.abstract: While the general idea of self-supervised learning is identical across modalities, the actual algorithms and objectives differ widely because they were developed with a single modality in mind. To get us closer to general self-supervised learning, we present data2vec, a framework that uses the same learning method for either speech, NLP or computer vision. The core idea is to predict latent representations of the full input data based on a masked view of the input in a self-distillation setup using a standard Transformer architecture. Instead of predicting modality-specific targets such as words, visual tokens or units of human speech which are local in nature, data2vec predicts contextualized latent representations that contain information from the entire input. Experiments on the major benchmarks of speech recognition, image classification, and natural language understanding demonstrate a new state of the art or competitive performance to predominant approaches.

\begin{abstract}
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) has demonstrated strong performance in speech processing, particularly in automatic speech recognition. In this paper, we explore an SSL pretraining framework that leverages masked language modeling with targets derived from a speech recognition model. We also present chunkwise attention with dynamic chunk size sampling during pretraining to enable both full-context and streaming fine-tuning. Our experiments examine scaling with respect to model size and the amount of data. Using our method, we train the GigaAM family of models, including a state-of-the-art model for Russian speech recognition that outperforms Whisper-large-v3 by $50\%$. We have released our foundation and ASR models, along with the inference code, under the MIT license as open-source resources to the research community. Available at https://github.com/salute-developers/gigaam.
\end{abstract}

Self-supervised learning (SSL) has transformed ASR by leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data, reducing the need for manual annotation. Numerous methods have emerged \cite{hubert, wavlm, bestrq, pbert, wav2vec2, wav2vec, data2vec}, but some of them suffer from training instability due to representation collapse \cite{hubert, wav2vec2, data2vec}. On the other hand, BEST-RQ \cite{bestrq} has proven effective due to its use of a frozen audio quantization module that provides targets for masked language prediction in a single stage. However, despite its training stability, BEST-RQ suffers from semantically uninformative targets because they are derived from low-level representations. Layer-wise analyses in the literature suggest that the most semantically rich features appear in the intermediate layers, while the final layers tend to exhibit an autoencoder-like behavior \cite{layer_analysis, best_rq_autoencoder}.

However, these approaches often suffer from training instability or representation collapse and require extensive hyperparameter tuning.

Motivated by these observations, we propose an SSL pretraining framework that overcomes these limitations. Our approach leverages semantically enriched target variables derived from a supervised ASR model. Furthermore, to address potential model degeneracy on excessive silence in the audio data, we preprocess it by removing segments with insufficient speech activity. In contrast to PBERT \cite{pbert}, which extracts targets from an intermediate layer, we perform K-means clustering on the last layer of a CTC-based ASR model \cite{ctcloss} to generate targets that capture higher-level semantic information.

In addition, we explored chunk size sampling during both pretraining and fine-tuning stages and found that a single pretraining run is sufficient to support both full-context and streaming ASR setups.

\section{Related Work}

The field of self-supervised learning for speech encompasses a wide range of methods, from early approaches such as wav2vec \cite{wav2vec} to more recent advances. Although many excellent techniques have been proposed, in this work we focus on two representative frameworks -- HuBERT \cite{hubert} and BEST-RQ -- due to their complementary strengths. HuBERT, which forms the basis of our approach, employs a multi-stage masked language modeling pipeline to learn robust representations. At the same time, BEST-RQ is widely used in production-scale systems for its efficient, single-stage pretraining via a frozen audio quantizer \cite{usm}. In the following subsections, we detail these two approaches and discuss how our method builds upon and extends their core ideas.

\subsection{SSL Pretraining: HuBERT vs. BEST-RQ}

In the HuBERT framework, discrete target tokens are generated through a multi-stage pipeline. Given an input sequence of audio features,
% \[
% \mathcal{X} = \{ x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T \},
% \]
a subset of time indices is selected for masking.
% \[
% \mathcal{M} = \{ t_1^{mask}, t_2^{mask}, \dots, t_m^{mask} \}.
% \]
At these masked positions, the input features are replaced with a predefined mask embedding. In Stage 1, K-means clustering is applied to low-level features (e.g., MFCCs) to assign each frame a token corresponding to its nearest centroid. In Stage 2, the clustering is repeated on the intermediate representations of a pretrained (teacher) model to yield refined assignments. By contrast, BEST-RQ employs random vector quantization with frozen codebooks and projection module. This approach avoids representation collapse issues observed in jointly trained models such as wav2vec2 \cite{wav2vec2} and w2v-BERT \cite{w2v-bert}.

\subsection{Importance of Data Domain in Pretraining}

The pre-training data selection process is critical for downstream ASR performance. Prior work has shown that domain-specific models can outperform multilingual ones. For example, Babu et al. \cite{xlsr} demonstrated that monolingual models yield superior performance on domain-specific tasks, and Lu et al. \cite{google_data_selection} reported that filtering the pretraining data to match the target domain can lead to up to a $15\%$ relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER). Motivated by these findings, our approach pretrains exclusively on Russian speech to ensure that the learned representations are optimally adapted to the target domain.

\subsection{Chunkwise Attention Mechanisms}

In practice, ASR models are often trained on relatively short audio segments (e.g., up to $30$ seconds), which can be problematic when operating in a long-form scenario. For instance, a full-context model trained on $30$-second audio fragments might struggle when presented with a $2$-minute audio file. To address this, we employ a chunkwise attention mechanism that divides the input into fixed-length segments.

Formally, given an input sequence
% \[
% \mathcal{X} = \{ x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T \},
% \]
and a predefined chunk size (e.g., $200$ms, $1$s, $2$s, $4$s, or $8$s), we partition the sequence into consecutive segments of the selected length.
% \[
% \mathcal{X}_c^{(i)} = \{ x_{(i-1)c+1}, x_{(i-1)c+2}, \dots, x_{ic} \}.
% \]
Within each chunk, attention is computed locally, enabling the model to focus on limited context rather than the entire sequence. This not only helps in generalizing to longer audio inputs but also supports streaming scenarios where only limited future context is available. We further incorporate dynamic chunk size sampling during pretraining so that the model learns to adapt to varying context lengths, allowing it to perform effectively in both full-context and streaming setups without requiring expensive re-training runs.

\subsection{Scaling Laws in SSL Pretraining}

Scaling laws have been extensively studied in natural language processing \cite{Kaplan2020, Hoffmann2022} and computer vision \cite{Dosovitskiy2021}, yet systematic investigations for self-supervised ASR remain limited. While previous works \cite{google_10b, fair_scaling, whisper} has examined the influence of model capacity, the amount of training data, and compute budget in multilingual and semi-supervised settings, a comprehensive analysis for self-supervised pretraining is still needed. In this work, we analyze scaling effects by varying the number of pretraining steps, the pretraining dataset size (spanning two orders of magnitude), the fine-tuning dataset size (spanning three orders of magnitude), and the model capacity (spanning 1.5 orders of magnitude), and we observe how these factors influence the performance of our SSL model on downstream task.
